base_method_text.title:
Characteristic Guidance: Non-linear Correction for Diffusion Model at
  Large Guidance Scale
base_method_text.summary:
Popular guidance for denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) linearly
combines distinct conditional models together to provide enhanced control over
samples. However, this approach overlooks nonlinear effects that become
significant when guidance scale is large. To address this issue, we propose
characteristic guidance, a guidance method that provides first-principle
non-linear correction for classifier-free guidance. Such correction forces the
guided DDPMs to respect the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation of diffusion process,
in a way that is training-free and compatible with existing sampling methods.
Experiments show that characteristic guidance enhances semantic characteristics
of prompts and mitigate irregularities in image generation, proving effective
in diverse applications ranging from simulating magnet phase transitions to
latent space sampling.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces 'characteristic guidance,' a novel non-linear correction method for classifier-free guided Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs). It addresses the issue of irregularities in image generation at large guidance scales by enforcing adherence to the Fokker-Planck equation, enhancing semantic characteristics, and mitigating color and exposure issues without requiring additional training.
base_method_text.methodology: The core of the method involves a non-linear correction term (∆x) applied to the classifier-free guidance, derived by solving the score Fokker-Planck equation using the method of characteristics under a Harmonic ansatz. This correction is implemented through fixed-point iteration algorithms, with orthogonal projections used to accelerate computation and regularize the solution.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on various datasets: conditional 2D Gaussian distributions, a mixture of Gaussian distributions, CIFAR-10, ImageNet 256, and Stable Diffusion. The method was evaluated using metrics like Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, Frechet Inception Distance (FID), Inception Score (IS), and visual inspection. It was also tested on simulating magnet phase transitions using the Landau-Ginzburg model.
base_method_text.limitations: The effectiveness of FID as an evaluation metric is compromised by the difference between the target conditional probabilities and marginal probabilities. The iterative computation of the non-linear correction can be slow, and advanced regularization techniques are needed to enhance the convergence rate and accelerate computation.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring advanced regularization techniques beyond projection to improve the convergence rate of the iterative correction. There is also a need for more appropriate metrics that account for the discrepancy between the target conditional probabilities and marginal probabilities in guided DDPMs.

add_method_texts.title:
Score identity Distillation: Exponentially Fast Distillation of
  Pretrained Diffusion Models for One-Step Generation
add_method_texts.summary:
We introduce Score identity Distillation (SiD), an innovative data-free
method that distills the generative capabilities of pretrained diffusion models
into a single-step generator. SiD not only facilitates an exponentially fast
reduction in Fr\'echet inception distance (FID) during distillation but also
approaches or even exceeds the FID performance of the original teacher
diffusion models. By reformulating forward diffusion processes as semi-implicit
distributions, we leverage three score-related identities to create an
innovative loss mechanism. This mechanism achieves rapid FID reduction by
training the generator using its own synthesized images, eliminating the need
for real data or reverse-diffusion-based generation, all accomplished within
significantly shortened generation time. Upon evaluation across four benchmark
datasets, the SiD algorithm demonstrates high iteration efficiency during
distillation and surpasses competing distillation approaches, whether they are
one-step or few-step, data-free, or dependent on training data, in terms of
generation quality. This achievement not only redefines the benchmarks for
efficiency and effectiveness in diffusion distillation but also in the broader
field of diffusion-based generation. The PyTorch implementation is available at
https://github.com/mingyuanzhou/SiD
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces Score identity Distillation (SiD), a data-free method for distilling pretrained diffusion models into a single-step generator. SiD achieves rapid reduction in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and can surpass the FID performance of the original teacher diffusion models. The method reformulates forward diffusion processes as semi-implicit distributions and uses score-related identities to create a novel loss mechanism.
add_method_texts.methodology: SiD leverages three score-related identities derived from reformulating forward diffusion processes as semi-implicit distributions. It employs a model-based score-matching loss, specifically a variant of Fisher divergence, approximated using Monte Carlo estimation techniques. The generator is trained using its own synthesized images, eliminating the need for real data or reverse diffusion.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The method was evaluated on four benchmark datasets: CIFAR-10 32x32, ImageNet 64x64, FFHQ 64x64, and AFHQv2 64x64. VP-EDM checkpoints were used as teacher diffusion models. Performance was measured using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS). Precision and Recall were also considered for ImageNet 64x64.
add_method_texts.limitations: SiD requires managing three networks simultaneously during distillation, increasing memory demands compared to traditional diffusion model training. The method also has increased memory allocation and iteration time compared to Diff-Instruct, due to the computation of score gradients.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring the use of LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce the memory footprint of the generator score network and the generator. Additionally, more advanced strategies such as progressively increasing the batch size, annealing the learning rate, and implementing gradient clipping could be explored. Further investigation into reasons for divergence in ImageNet 64x64 training is also warranted.

base_experimental_code:
The repository contains code for implementing classifier-free diffusion guidance using PyTorch. The core components include:

1.  **Scheduler.py**: Implements a GradualWarmupScheduler for controlling the learning rate during training.
2.  **diffusion.py**: Defines the GaussianDiffusion class, which implements the forward and reverse diffusion processes, including:
    *   Calculation of parameters for the forward diffusion process q(xₜ|x₀).
    *   Sampling from q(xₜ|x₀).
    *   Calculation of parameters for the posterior q(xₜ₋₁|xₜ, x₀).
    *   Sampling from the conditional distribution p(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) using the learned model.
    *   DDIM sampling for faster generation.
    *   Loss calculation for training the diffusion model.
3.  **embedding.py**: Defines a ConditionalEmbedding module for embedding class labels.
4.  **unet.py**: Defines the UNet architecture used as the noise predictor in the diffusion model.
5.  **sample.py**: Implements the sampling procedure using the trained diffusion model.
6.  **train.py**: Contains the training loop for the diffusion model, including data loading, model setup, optimization, and checkpointing.
7.  **dataloader_cifar.py**: Defines the data loading pipeline for CIFAR-10.
8.  **utils.py**: Provides utility functions, such as a function for generating beta schedules.

Key functions and classes related to the diffusion process include:

*   `GaussianDiffusion` class in `diffusion.py` which encapsulates the diffusion process.
*   `p_mean_variance` and `p_sample` functions for reverse diffusion.
*   `ddim_p_sample` and `ddim_sample` for DDIM sampling.
*   `training_loss` for calculating the loss during training.
*   `UNet` class in `unet.py` represents the noise prediction model.
base_experimental_info:
The experimental setup involves training and sampling from a diffusion model, primarily on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Key aspects of the experimental setup include:

1.  **Dataset**: CIFAR-10 is used for training and evaluation (specified in `dataloader_cifar.py`).
2.  **Model Architecture**: A UNet architecture (defined in `unet.py`) is employed as the noise prediction network. The architecture's parameters, such as channel multipliers (`ch_mul`), number of residual blocks (`num_res_blocks`), and use of convolution in downsampling (`use_conv`), are configurable via command-line arguments.
3.  **Training Details**: Training is performed using the AdamW optimizer with a cosine annealing learning rate schedule (managed by `Scheduler.py`).  Gradient warm-up is also employed. DistributedDataParallel (DDP) is used for multi-GPU training.
4.  **Diffusion Parameters**: A linear beta schedule (configured in `utils.py`) is used for the diffusion process. The number of diffusion timesteps (`T`) is a configurable parameter.
5.  **Conditional Generation**: Class labels are embedded using a `ConditionalEmbedding` module (defined in `embedding.py`) and provided as input to the UNet, enabling class-conditional image generation.
6.  **Classifier-Free Guidance**: The code implements classifier-free guidance, with the guidance strength (`w`) being a configurable hyperparameter.
7.  **Sampling**: Images are sampled from the trained model using either the standard reverse diffusion process or DDIM sampling for faster generation. The number of sampling steps and the DDIM eta value are configurable parameters.
8.  **Evaluation**:  The code includes an option to generate samples for quantitative evaluation using FID (Fréchet Inception Distance), although the specific FID calculation is not included in the provided code. Visual inspection of generated samples is also implicitly part of the evaluation.
9.  **Command-line Arguments**: The `train.py` and `sample.py` scripts use `argparse` to provide a wide range of configurable hyperparameters, including batch sizes, learning rates, model architecture parameters, diffusion parameters, and sampling parameters.
new_method:
Below is the outcome of step 3—a proposal for a genuinely new method inspired by both the Base Method and the selected Add Method approach:

─────────────────────────────  
Proposed Method: Score Identity-Corrected Guidance (SICG)

Overview:  
SICG is designed to combine the powerful non-linear correction of the Base Method’s characteristic guidance with the rapid, one-step generation benefits of Score Identity Distillation (SiD). The goal is to overcome the Base Method’s iterative computational overhead and convergence issues while retaining robust, high-scale guidance behavior. Instead of applying a fixed-point iterative correction at inference time, SICG embeds the non-linear correction into a fast, distilled network that bypasses slow iterative processes.

How SICG Works:  

1. Teacher-Driven Nonlinear Correction:  
 • First, follow the Base Method by computing the non-linear correction term (∆x) using the characteristic guidance that enforces adherence to the Fokker–Planck equation via fixed-point iterations.  
 • This teacher “oracle” captures complex correction dynamics, particularly at large guidance scales that emphasize semantic consistency and mitigate irregularities.

2. Distillation via Score Identity Loss:  
 • Inspired by SiD, a “student” network is then trained to mimic the teacher’s correction behavior. The student network receives as input the noisy sample (or its latent representation) along with guidance information, and predicts the correction Δx in a single forward pass.  
 • The training objective includes score identity losses (e.g., a loss based on Fisher divergence) that encourage the student’s predictions to satisfy inherent score-related identities from the underlying diffusion process. Additionally, Monte Carlo sampling can be used to approximate the expected score errors.

3. Semi-Implicit Reformulation for Stability:  
 • Drawing further from SiD’s reformulation of forward processes as semi-implicit distributions, SICG reformulates the forward diffusion and associated correction dynamics. This promotes a stable loss landscape during distillation and helps the student network generalize well to diverse conditions and high guidance scales.

4. Inference with One-Step Correction:  
 • At inference, instead of running iterative fixed-point iterations, the student network instantly computes the ∆x correction, yielding one-shot, high-quality guided image generations. This significantly reduces the computational overhead while still producing the semantic robustness and regularity improvements of the Base Method.

Benefits and Innovations:  
• Speed: The heavy iterative computation of the original non-linear correction is offloaded during a one-time distillation process, leading to near-instantaneous correction at generation time.  
• Robust Guidance: By training on the teacher’s characteristic actions, the distilled student retains the semantic integrity and improved image quality under large guidance scales.  
• Reduced Runtime Complexity: SICG offers a scalable alternative, especially when fast inference is required or when computational resources are limited.  
• Theoretically Sound: The method naturally embeds score identity constraints within the training loss, ensuring consistency with diffusion theory while benefiting from the practical speed-up of distillation.

In summary, Score Identity-Corrected Guidance leverages the high-quality, non-linear correction from the Base Method and marries it with the efficiency of score identity distillation. This novel approach addresses the iterative slowness and convergence issues of the Base Method while maintaining, and potentially enhancing, the semantic and fidelity improvements during image generation at large guidance scales.

related_papers.title: A Survey on Recent Teacher-student Learning Studies

summary.main_contributions: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent teacher-student learning methods, specifically focusing on various knowledge distillation (KD) variants. It revisits and extends traditional KD by exploring techniques such as teacher assistant distillation, curriculum distillation, mask distillation, decoupling distillation, as well as novel approaches like inverse probability weighted distillation (IPWD), early-stopped KD, decoupled KD (DKD), asymmetric temperature scaling (ATS), DIST, course temperature KD (CTKD), masked generative distillation (MGD), and simple KD (SimKD). The key contribution is the systematic analysis and comparison of these variants and their potential to enhance the performance and efficiency of knowledge transfer from large teacher models to smaller student models.
summary.methodology: The paper reviews several methodological improvements over classical KD. These include using an intermediate teaching assistant network to bridge capacity gaps, curriculum strategies that progressively increase learning difficulty, masking strategies to capture attention mechanisms, decoupling the distillation loss from task loss, and weighting schemes to handle class imbalance. Additionally, it introduces techniques such as inverse probability weighting, asymmetric temperature scaling to adjust logits, and the DIST method using correlation-based losses for intra-class and inter-class relations. The approaches are implemented via modifications to loss functions, network design, and gradient inversion techniques.
summary.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on multiple standard datasets and benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet (for image classification), MS-COCO (for object detection and instance segmentation), and CityScapes (for semantic segmentation). The evaluation metrics include classification accuracy, mean Average Precision (mAP) for detection tasks, and Intersection over Union (IoU) for segmentation tasks. A variety of student and teacher architectures (e.g., ResNet, WideResNet, VGG, MobileNet, and transformer-based models) were used to validate the proposed techniques.
summary.limitations: The paper acknowledges several limitations, such as the increased computational cost when using multiple distillation stages (especially for teacher assistant based methods), challenges in adapting methods when teacher and student architectures differ significantly, and instances where some techniques (e.g., DKD in target detection) do not outperform state-of-the-art feature-based methods. Additionally, the dependency on carefully tuned hyperparameters and the potential transfer gap due to teacher over-confidence are noted as constraints.
summary.future_research_directions: Not mentioned explicitly in the text but implied directions include further exploration of balancing teacher-student capacity differences, reducing computational overhead, improving hyperparameter optimization, and combining multiple KD variants to further boost performance. There is also room for investigating the underlying reasons why larger teachers do not always yield better student performance, as well as expanding these methods to more diverse tasks and architectures within deep learning applications in computer vision and natural language processing.

related_papers.title:
Characteristic Guidance: Non-linear Correction for Diffusion Model at
  Large Guidance Scale

summary.main_contributions: The paper addresses the degradation of sample quality in diffusion models when using large guidance scales, by identifying the non-linear effects ignored by classifier‐free guidance. It introduces 'characteristic guidance' which applies a first-principle non-linear correction based on the Fokker–Planck equation (via the method of characteristics) in a training-free manner, ensuring better semantic consistency and reduced artifacts.
summary.methodology: The approach derives a corrected denoising network by solving the Fokker–Planck equation under a harmonic ansatz using the method of characteristics. The paper formulates an analytical relation between conditional, unconditional, and guided networks, and then computes a non-linear correction term using fixed-point iterative methods (including gradient descent, RMSprop, and Anderson acceleration) with an optional projection operator for regularization.
summary.experimental_setup: Experiments span both synthetic and real-world scenarios: conditional Gaussian distributions and mixtures of Gaussians for theoretical validation, as well as standard datasets like CIFAR-10, ImageNet256, and latent space models in Stable Diffusion. Various sampling methods (SDE, probabilistic ODE, DDIM, and DPM++2M) are utilized, with performance evaluated using metrics such as KL divergence, FID, Inception Score, and Negative Log-Likelihood, complemented by visual inspection.
summary.limitations: The method depends on the harmonic ansatz, which may not hold in overlapping regions of complex distributions leading to minor artifacts. Additionally, the iterative process for computing the correction term can be computationally demanding, and conventional evaluation metrics like FID may not fully reflect improvements in conditional guidance quality.
summary.future_research_directions: Exploration of advanced regularization techniques for faster convergence of the iterative correction, development of more suitable evaluation metrics for guided DDPMs, and extending the approach to further non-linear scenarios beyond the harmonic ansatz would be promising future directions. Furthermore, integration and optimization in diverse modalities and real-world tasks could be explored in subsequent work.

summary.main_contributions: The paper introduces the Target Score Identity (TSI) and the corresponding Target Score Matching (TSM) loss, which leverage explicit knowledge of the clean target's score to improve score estimation in denoising diffusion models. This approach addresses the high variance issues of traditional Denoising Score Matching, especially at low noise levels.
summary.methodology: The authors derive a new score identity (TSI) showing that the score of the noised distribution can be expressed as the expectation of the clean target’s score under the posterior. Based on this, they design the TSM regression loss, which minimizes the squared error between the estimated score and the known target score. Extensions are provided for non-additive noise models, Lie groups, and bridge matching settings, with techniques such as importance sampling, Monte Carlo approximation, and the use of analytical derivations.
summary.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data including one-dimensional mixtures of Gaussians (unit Gaussian, easy mixture, and hard mixtures with same or different variances) and two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures. The experimental evaluation focuses on analyzing Monte Carlo estimator variance and the behavior of different score matching losses, with an MLP architecture utilized for the score model and diffusion processes scheduled as in prior literature.
summary.limitations: The approach relies on having explicit knowledge of the clean target score, which may limit its applicability to domains where this information is available. Additionally, the theoretical derivations and experimental validations are primarily focused on additive noise scenarios, and extensions to more complex or real-world noise models may require further adaptation.

related_papers.title:
DisjunctiveProgramming.jl: Generalized Disjunctive Programming Models
  and Algorithms for JuMP

summary.main_contributions: The paper introduces DisjunctiveProgramming.jl, a Julia package that extends JuMP to model optimization problems using logical propositions and disjunctive constraints. It enables the creation of Generalized Disjunctive Programming (GDP) models that can be reformulated into Mixed-Integer Programs (MIPs) using methods like Big-M and Hull reformulations.
summary.methodology: The work leverages reformulation techniques by converting logical propositions to Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) and using Big-M and Hull reformulations to transform disjunctive constraints into algebraic MIP constraints. It also discusses solution strategies including disjunctive branch and bound, logic-based outer approximation, and hybrid cutting planes, and utilizes macros (e.g., @disjunction, @proposition) to facilitate model development.
summary.experimental_setup: An illustrative case study on chemical process superstructure optimization is presented, where a chemical plant design problem with nested disjunctions is modeled and solved using the HiGHS MILP solver. The framework is demonstrated through example optimization problems rather than using extensive datasets or benchmarks.
summary.limitations: The paper notes challenges such as determining tight Big-M values (especially for nonlinear constraints) and the increased model complexity associated with the Hull reformulation. The current implementation might also be constrained by available GDP solution strategies and could benefit from further enhancements in flexibility and performance.
summary.future_research_directions: Future work aims to extend DisjunctiveProgramming.jl by integrating more direct GDP solution strategies without pre-reformulation, improving support for disjunction indexing, introducing a dedicated Boolean variable type, and enhancing performance for advanced applications of GDP in JuMP models. This will make the package more usable and flexible for a wider range of industries and academic research programs. (Not mentioned explicitly as existing research relevance but implied as an extension.)

summary.main_contributions: The paper introduces spine-local type inference, a variant of local type inference for System F that extends type-argument inference beyond a single AST node, enabling first-class curried applications, partial type applications, and inferring types for terms that conventional local type inference fails to handle.
summary.methodology: The authors build on bidirectional type inference and incorporate contextual type-argument inference within an application spine. They specify the system via formal inference rules, including both a specification and an algorithmic version that employs prototypes, decorated types, and a prototype matching algorithm to generate substitutions and elaborate terms.
summary.experimental_setup: The paper primarily presents theoretical derivations and examples (such as typing derivations for expressions like pair (λ x .x) z), rather than empirical evaluation with datasets or benchmarks.
summary.limitations: The approach still requires some type annotations in cases where local information is insufficient (e.g., bare lambda abstractions). Additionally, the system may encounter limitations in greedy instantiation and potential ambiguity when extended to richer type systems with subtyping, requiring further annotations from the programmer.
summary.future_research_directions: Potential directions include extending the system to handle subtyping more gracefully and refining the algorithm to reduce annotation requirements further, as well as integrating these inference techniques into practical implementations such as the Cedille language compiler to enhance usability for advanced type features.
